lines.text: Now turn to Section Four. You will hear part of a lecture on the decline of urban bee populations.

Questions thirty-one to thirty-four. Complete the summary below. Write no more than two words and/or a number for each answer. First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to thirty-four.
Now listen and answer questions thirty-one to thirty-four.
Today I want to talk about a subject that's become increasingly urgent in ecology: the decline of bee populations in urban areas.
Globally, bee populations are thought to have declined by around thirty percent over the last two decades.
There are several contributing factors, but the research points to three in particular: habitat loss, pesticide exposure, and a parasite known as the varroa mite.
Of these, the mite is especially damaging, because it weakens the bees' immune system, leaving colonies far more vulnerable to disease.
Now, why does this matter beyond the insects themselves? Bees are responsible for pollinating roughly one third of the food crops we consume.
Questions thirty-five and thirty-six. Choose the correct letter, A, B or C. First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-five and thirty-six.
Now listen and answer questions thirty-five and thirty-six.
In response, a number of cities have launched schemes that encourage ordinary residents to keep bees on rooftops and in private gardens.
One of the clearest examples of this has been in the city of Manchester, which researchers now treat as a case study rather than a one-off local project.
Questions thirty-seven to forty. Complete the notes below. Write no more than two words and/or a number for each answer. First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-seven to forty.
Now listen and answer questions thirty-seven to forty.
There, the number of rooftop hives has tripled since 2015, largely thanks to a council-backed initiative offering free training to new beekeepers.
Researchers in the same city also introduced pollinator corridors — narrow strips of wildflowers planted along roads and railway lines.
The idea is simple: to give bees safe routes to travel between larger green spaces, rather than having to cross exposed, built-up areas.
Much of this work has been funded by the Greenfield Environmental Trust, a charity dedicated to urban conservation projects.
Next week, we'll build on this by looking at policy responses to bee decline across several different countries. Thank you.
That is the end of the Listening test.
